entries.title: Israeli strikes kill at least three, including UNRWA worker, in Gaza
entries.summary: Israel continues to launch attacks across the enclave, despite an October 2025 'ceasefire' deal.
entries.content:
Israel continues to launch attacks across the enclave, despite an October 2025 ‘ceasefire’ deal.

Israeli air strikes have killed at least three people in Gaza, including a worker for the UN Palestinian refugee agency, according to the relief agency and local health officials.

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) on Monday named the worker killed as Adel al-Helo.

He was working near a well in the Jabalia refugee camp in the enclave’s north when hit, the agency and medics said. Three others were wounded in the strike.

Later on Monday, another Israeli air strike ⁠targeted a vehicle in western Gaza City, killing two people and wounding others, medics said, according to the Reuters news agency. The Israeli military did not immediately comment.

Israel continues to launch attacks across the enclave, despite an October 2025 “ceasefire” deal with Hamas, which formally halted around two years of fighting but has failed to bring Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza to an end.

“The initial reports indicate that the strike hit a target on the street near the water well, which was manned by UNRWA staff and a guard. The staff were engaged in their regular duties associated with water well operations,” an UNRWA spokesperson told Reuters.

Israel has yet to respond to the incident. But since the October ceasefire, at least 1,679 Palestinian people and five Israeli soldiers have been killed.

Israeli forces have also continued to destroy residential buildings in Gaza, beyond the “Yellow Line” to which they were required to withdraw under the ceasefire.

Al Jazeera journalist Moath al-Kahlout, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said displaced Palestinians who live in the area near the line gathered on Saturday to demonstrate against Israel’s intensifying air strikes.

“More than 500 housing units have been destroyed in less than a month,” Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir el-Balah’s Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera.

“This is part of what appears to be a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement aimed at forcing residents out of their camp and destroying as many homes as possible,” he added.

entries.title: Russia warns Ukraine of ‘dangerous trend’ after Libya and Baltic attacks
entries.summary: Russia has reacted with fury to Ukraine's continued campaign targeting its naval and merchant shipping.
entries.content:
Moscow has reacted with fury to Kyiv’s continued campaign targeting its naval and merchant shipping.

Moscow has warned Ukraine that it will face “painful consequences” for its drone attacks on Russian vessels in Libya and the Baltic Sea.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that Russia’s Ministry of Defence was handling the matter after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country’s forces had sunk two ships in the Libyan port of Benghazi.

Peskov said the ministry would release details if it deemed it appropriate, adding that Russia will continue its attacks on Ukraine in response.

“Our military personnel continue to carry out large-scale, comprehensive strikes on military infrastructure in Ukraine on a daily basis. This practice has very painful consequences for the Kyiv regime,” he said.

Peskov added that the Baltic attack was “escalating tensions” in the region while he said Moscow hoped the Baltic states would use their influence to press Kyiv to stop what he described as “terrorist practices”.

Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukrainian forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury at a naval base in Benghazi on Sunday and struck a cargo ship he said Russia used to carry weapons.

Libya’s eastern-based government, a rival to the country’s internationally recognised western government in Tripoli, has lodged a complaint with the United Nations, saying the attacks violated Libyan sovereignty. It called for an international investigation into reports that Ukrainian military personnel were allegedly present in western Libya.

The attacks are part of Ukraine’s increased efforts to target naval assets and merchant ships linked to Moscow’s “shadow fleet”, which is used to help Russia evade Western sanctions.

A drone attack on Saturday set the Kaliningrad-bound Sparta II on fire in international waters in the Baltic Sea. Finland’s military said Ukraine likely carried out the attack.

Peskov also hit out at that attack, saying it marked a “very dangerous trend”.

The attack exposed Russia’s growing reliance on maritime transport.

On Monday, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said Moscow would spend 47 billion roubles ($576m) on two rail ferries to keep goods flowing to the exclave of Kaliningrad, which sits on the Baltic Sea coast between Lithuania and Poland, isolated from mainland Russia.

Lithuania restricted the transit of goods, including construction materials, from Russia to the exclave in line with European Union sanctions in 2022, leaving Kaliningrad heavily dependent on sea-borne supplies.

The ferries are expected to begin running between Ust-Luga and Baltiysk in 2030. Russia’s rainy-day fund will cover most of the cost, Mishustin said.

Nuclear sabre rattling

As so often, amid the rhetoric, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev sought to up the ante, repeating his regular nuclear sabre rattling.

“Russia has the right, and in some circumstances the obligation, to use every means at its disposal to defend itself, potentially including nuclear weapons,” the former president wrote in an article published on Monday.

However, he conceded that while Ukraine and NATO countries continue to provoke Moscow, it has so far not seen a “direct necessity” to use nuclear weapons in its war in Ukraine.

entries.title: Police investigating bomb threats against schools in Germany and Denmark
entries.summary: Bomb threats follow hoax emails sent to schools across Europe earlier in November.
entries.content:
Bomb threats follow hoax emails sent to schools across Europe earlier in November.

Police are investigating bomb threats made against schools across Germany and Denmark.

Schools in the German capital, Berlin, and Danish capital, Copenhagen, were among those targeted, authorities said on Monday. The warnings, which were delivered via email, came after a wave of bomb threats across Europe earlier this month.

As well as the capital, German police said schools in the states of Baden-Wurttemberg, Thuringia, Saxony-Anhalt and Rhineland-Palatinate were among the 450 schools affected across the country.

It was quickly concluded that the threats did not represent a “concrete danger” and were “not serious”, they added.

“At present, there is no evidence to suggest that the schools contacted so far are facing any specific threat,” police in the southwestern city of Freiburg in Baden-Wurttemberg said in a statement. Berlin police gave similar advice.

Authorities in the state of Thuringia said separately that they told schools to continue as normal because the perpetrators’ apparent intention was to scare people without taking action.

Police in the western state of Rhineland-Palatinate said in the “largely identical emails”, anonymous authors “claim to have placed explosive devices in school buildings and threatened to detonate them”.

The tabloid Bild reported that the subject of the emailed threat was: “Death awaits you.”

A Ministry of the Interior spokesman said schools were not being advised to evacuate because the incident fits into “the current overall threat picture”.

“I think both the schools and the security authorities of the federal states are prepared for such incidents and can then respond in a way that is appropriate to the situation,” he told reporters in Berlin, declining to comment on who might be behind the incident.

Danish police also said there was no danger as they investigated bomb threats directed at schools across the country, public broadcaster DR reported.

“We fully understand that this may cause concern,” Copenhagen Police said in a statement, adding that police officers are in dialogue with the municipalities and several of the schools.

According to the report, schools across Bornholm, Funen and Jutland as well as in Herning were among those that received bomb threats.

Disruption

Hoaxes and cyberattacks have hit schools, supermarkets, blood banks, air traffic systems and broadcasters across Europe in recent weeks.

Last week, more than 10 schools in Spain were evacuated after receiving bomb threats by email.

Schools in Italy were evacuated earlier in the month after thousands received emailed bomb threats.

In recent weeks, schools in Britain, Hungary and Serbia have also been sent hoax bomb threats.

entries.title: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
entries.summary: Huang stepped down earlier this month after revelations of at least two affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy.
entries.content:
Huang stepped down earlier this month after revelations of at least two affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang is returning to Nvidia as chief executive, a little more than a week after he resigned amid extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

On Monday, the tech giant’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement as the company announced his return.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.”

Nvidia said that Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as chief financial officer.

United States President Donald Trump welcomed the decision in a post on social media.

“The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

Huang’s resignation on November 12 prompted immediate pushback from Silicon Valley insiders. Within days of his departure, a petition calling for his return had drawn more than 180,000 signatures, including from SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.

He was reinstated despite multiple investigations into the chipmaker, including by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Department of Justice (DOJ), which are still ongoing.

Wall Street responds

Nvidia shares jumped by more than 33 percent on the news as US markets opened on Monday.

Analysts also praised the decision. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera Huang’s return was a “huge positive”.

“Founders like Jensen are irreplaceable. They bring unparalleled vision, execution and grit. Hard to overstate how important this is for America winning the [super intelligence] race, Nvidia, and innovation in general,” Monaghan said.

“At the end of the day, despite this Jensen saga, the board knew it had no choice but to bring him back, and for the US technology sector, this was the move it had to make,” Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in a note on Monday.

Ives previously said that Nvidia could lose as much as 30 percent of its value without Huang.

Market volatility

The decision coincides with a volatile period for the artificial intelligence (AI) sector following the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats – many of whom are more sceptical of AI – won control of Congress. The elections also saw ballot measures aimed at restricting data centre development passed in all but one vote.

Last week, Anthropic made its blockbuster Wall Street debut, with shares surging 34 percent from their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83 to $111.50 when trading began. Since then, however, the stock has fallen more than 16 percent.

Nvidia and Anthropic have close financial ties. Nvidia committed $10bn to Anthropic’s IPO, in addition to a separate $10bn investment announced in 2025.

The news has boosted the broader market, which had slumped last week. On Monday, all the major US indices were trending upwards. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was up 6.7 percent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 2.8 percent and the S&P 500 was up 4.6 percent in early trading.
